newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic's coalition headed to victory.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic's coalition headed to victory.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's leftist coalition said on Monday it was headed to a comfortable victory, winning popular endorsement for his new peace-making policies despite a troubled economy.

"It is not a question whether we are going to win. It is rather the question of how resounding our victory will be," Slobodan Cerovic, a leading member of the influential coalition partner Yugoslav United Left (JUL), told Reuters.

Cerovic spoke after initial results of federal and municipal elections indicated Milosevic's coalition would prevail in rump Yugoslavia's first elections since the end of four years of war in the Balkans.
The leftist coalition is comprised of the JUL, headed by Milosevic's powerful wife Mirjana Markovic, New Democracy and Milosevic's Socialist Party, the SPS.

According to partial results from the federal and municipal elections, announced by SPS spokesman Ivica Dacic, the left was leading in nearly all major towns in Serbia and Montenegro, the two remaining Yugoslav republics.

Out of 2.2 million ballots counted, the leftist coalition had 1,093,234 votes, about 48 percent, the opposition coalition had 512,131 votes, about 23 percent, and the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party (SRS) had 406,967 votes, 18 percent.
It was a suprisingly strong showing for the hardline natioanalists in the SRS, which fell out with Milosevic over his decision to make concessions in peace negotiations.

In Montenegro, the Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS), allied with Milosevic's coalition, officially proclaimed victory in the republic's parliamentary elections, celebrating it with a fireworks display overnight in Podgorica.
According to partial results, the ruling party was in a convincing lead in 11 of 14 electoral districts in Montenegro, the state news agency Tanjug reported.
Leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition privately admitted defeat.
"I would be ecstatic if we were to get 40 percent of the votes," one, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
Opposition leaders blamed the state-run media, a boycott by ethnic Albanians, lack of interest by the West and voter apathy for their poor performance.
A low voter turnout of 61 percent in Serbia and 67 percent in Montenegro, reported by the federal election commission, was bad news for the opposition.
Milosevic's coalition parties rely on loyal followers -- many of them pensioners -- with disciplined voting habits.
Ironically, Milosevic had already been helped by his foes.

The ethnic Albanian majority in Kosovo and its fringe areas, which account for 15 of the 108 seats Serbia has in the 138-seat federal parliament, helped his candidates to romp home by boycotting the polls.

"They gave him a 15-0 head start over us. Its just like (Kosovo Albanian leader Ibrahim) Rugova joined a coalition with Milosevic," said Milan Bozic, political adviser to Vuk Draskovic, leader of the biggest opposition party, the SPO.

A team of election observers from the United States and several other states from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) monitored voting at some of the 10,000 polling stations.
During the campaign opposition leaders were virtually shut out of the state media and were able to reach voters only through rallies and a handful of independent papers.
The low turnout reflected widespread resignation in Yugoslavia, where almost a third of the people now live in poverty, according to a Red Cross survey.
A year of peace and the end of a U.N. trade embargo has failed to bring economic relief to a country which once enjoyed the highest standard of living in Eastern Europe.
The elections were the first major test for Milosevic's new peace-making policies, highlighted as the leading achievement by the ruling coalition to cover up miserable living standards.

Although Milosevic was not a candidate in the polls, an election victory for his parties should enable him to push through constitutional changes enabling him to stay in power after his second and final term as president expires next year.
Diplomats say he will probably assume the post of federal president after the next federal parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.
